key_concept: Population interactions are classified by their effect on each species: competition $(-,-)$, predation $(+,-)$, mutualism $(+,+)$ and commensalism $(+,0)$.
steps: A. Both species are harmed $(-,-)$. This is competition, because both species lose fitness while using the same limited resource. So A–III.
B. One species is harmed and the other benefits $(+,-)$. This is predation: the predator gains food and the prey is killed. So B–I.
C. Both species benefit $(+,+)$. This is mutualism, as in lichens, mycorrhizae or fig–wasp pollination. So C–II.
D. One species benefits and the other is unaffected $(+,0)$. This is commensalism, as in an orchid growing on a mango branch or barnacles on a whale. So D–IV.
The correct matching is A–III, B–I, C–II, D–IV, which is option (4).
why_not_others: Option (1) gives D to predation and B to commensalism, but commensalism has no harmed partner. Options (2) and (3) give A $(-,-)$ to predation or mutualism, even though neither involves harm to both species.
common_trap: Students confuse commensalism $(+,0)$ with predation or parasitism $(+,-)$. They forget that in commensalism the second species is neither harmed nor benefited.
time_saving_tip: Fix A–III first, since competition is the only $(-,-)$ interaction. This leaves options (1) and (4). Then B $(+,-)$ must be predation, which picks option (4).
